Imagine you worked your whole life, saved every month, and paid into a pension. Then, in about a year, all of it became worth less than a loaf of bread.
That is not a thought experiment. It happened to millions of people in Zimbabwe.
In January 2009, the central bank printed a single note worth one hundred trillion Zimbabwe dollars. On the day it came out, it was worth about thirty US dollars.
At the peak, economists estimate prices were doubling roughly every day. A shop could change its prices between breakfast and lunch.
And yet, not everyone was ruined. Some people came out of it fine. A few came out richer.
So in this video we'll answer three questions. How does a country with a strong currency end up printing trillion dollar notes?
What is daily life like when money stops working?
And when the money died, what actually survived? Because the answer says a lot about the money in your pocket today.
Rewind to 1980. Zimbabwe has just become independent, and its new currency is strong. On the official market, one Zimbabwe dollar is worth more than one US dollar.
The country has fertile land, gold and platinum in the ground, good roads, and a working banking system.
Its farms grow so much maize and tobacco that Zimbabwe is often called the breadbasket of southern Africa. It feeds itself and sells the rest abroad.

Those exports matter more than anything else in this story. Every crate of tobacco sold overseas brings home US dollars. And foreign dollars are what a country uses to buy fuel, medicine and machines it can't make itself.
Keep that in mind. Because when the dollars stop coming in, the trouble starts.
For most of the 1980s and early 1990s, the Zimbabwe dollar slowly weakened, like many currencies do. Nothing dramatic. Then came one Friday in 1997.

Crack number one. In 1997, the government promised large payouts and pensions to tens of thousands of veterans of the independence war. The money had not been budgeted. Nobody said where it would come from.
On the 14th of November 1997, investors gave their answer. The Zimbabwe dollar lost about seventy two percent of its value in a single day. People still call it Black Friday.
Crack number two. The next year, Zimbabwe sent about eleven thousand troops into the war in the Congo, hundreds of miles from home.

Officially it cost a few million dollars a month. Later, the finance minister admitted the real figure was closer to twenty three million US dollars a month, money a struggling budget simply didn't have.
Crack number three is the one that broke the foundation. Land.

Land ownership in Zimbabwe was very unequal, a legacy of colonial rule. Most of the best farmland was held in large commercial farms. Almost everyone agreed that had to change. The argument was about how.
From the year 2000, the government began taking large farms quickly, often by force, and handing the land to new owners. Supporters saw it as justice that was long overdue.
But many new farmers got land without seeds, tractors, irrigation, or bank loans. Without a title deed they could sell, banks wouldn't lend against the land either.
The numbers tell the story. In 1998, Zimbabwe grew about two hundred and sixty million kilograms of tobacco. By 2008 it was down to about forty eight million. A thirty year low.
Remember those export dollars? They dried up. Fewer crops meant fewer dollars, fewer dollars meant less fuel and fertiliser, and that meant even fewer crops.
So by the early 2000s, the government had big bills, a shrinking economy, and falling tax income. It had to find money somewhere. And it had a machine that could make it.
Every government that runs out of money faces the same temptation. You don't have to raise taxes or cut spending if you can just print the difference.
Zimbabwe's central bank started doing exactly that. It printed money to pay government salaries, to fund state companies, and to keep favoured businesses alive.

Part of the reason was the export problem from chapter two. With fewer dollars coming in from farms, the government couldn't pay its foreign bills either. So it printed local money and used it to buy whatever foreign dollars it could find, which pushed the Zimbabwe dollar down even faster.
Here's why that's a problem. Printing money doesn't create more bread, more fuel, or more houses. It just creates more pieces of paper chasing the same few goods.
So prices rise. People see prices rising and spend their money faster, before it loses value. That pushes prices up faster still. Economists call this the spiral, and once it starts, it feeds itself.
By 2006, the numbers on the notes were getting ridiculous. So the central bank simply removed three zeros. One new dollar replaced one thousand old ones.
It didn't help. Two years later, they removed ten more zeros. Then, in 2009, another twelve. Twenty five zeros wiped off the currency in under three years.
In June 2007, the government tried another fix. It ordered shops to cut their prices in half, and sent police to enforce it.

For a few days, it looked like a bargain. People rushed in and bought everything. Then the shelves were empty, because no shopkeeper could restock at a loss. Around thirteen hundred businesses were fined or charged.

Bread, sugar, cooking oil and fuel vanished from the shops, and reappeared on the black market at much higher prices. Price controls don't stop inflation. They just move it somewhere you can't see it.
In July 2008, the official statistics office reported annual inflation of two hundred and thirty one million percent. After that, it stopped publishing the figure.
Economists who kept counting, using exchange rates and share prices, estimate that by mid November 2008, prices were rising by seventy nine point six billion percent in a single month.
On a standard list of every hyperinflation in history, that's the second worst ever recorded. Only Hungary in 1946 was worse, when prices doubled about every fifteen hours.
And it led to that note. One hundred trillion dollars, printed in January 2009, worth about thirty US dollars on day one, and less every hour after that.
Chapter four. Life when money dies.
So what was it actually like to live through this?
If you got paid, you spent your wages the same day. Waiting until the weekend could cost you half of it.
People queued for hours at banks, because withdrawals were limited and the cash ran out. By the time you reached the front, your money had already lost value while you stood in line.
Big purchases were paid with bricks of notes, not single notes. Carrying enough cash for a week of groceries could mean carrying a bag full of paper.
Anyone who could, got paid in something else. US dollars, South African rand, or goods. Teachers, nurses and soldiers, paid in Zimbabwe dollars, watched their salaries become almost worthless.

Many Zimbabweans left the country to find work in South Africa, Botswana and Britain, and sent money home in foreign currency. For many families, those transfers were the only money that still worked.
Barter came back. A bag of maize meal, a tank of fuel, or a few litres of cooking oil became a kind of currency of their own, because everyone knew what they were worth.

And here's a strange detail. On paper, the Harare stock exchange was soaring. Share prices went up by enormous percentages. Not because companies were doing well, but because shares were one of the only things that kept up with the falling dollar.
Which brings us to the real question. If the money was dying, what kept its value?
Let's split everyone into two groups. People who held promises. And people who held things.
The first group held promises written in Zimbabwe dollars. Savings accounts, pensions, life insurance, government bonds, a fixed salary.
Every one of those is a promise to pay you a certain number of dollars later. When the dollar falls apart, the promise still gets kept, technically. It just pays you in paper that's worthless.

A government inquiry later estimated that more than three billion US dollars of pension and insurance value was wiped out. People who had saved responsibly for thirty years ended up with almost nothing.
The second group held things. Land, houses, cattle, gold, a working business, a stock of goods. You can't print more of any of those.
Real things kept their real value. A house in Harare was still a house. A cow was still a cow. In dollar terms their price went to the moon, but what they could buy stayed roughly the same.

Shares in real companies survived too. One insurer, Old Mutual, was listed in both Harare and London. Its shares held their value so reliably that economists used the gap between the two prices to measure how fast the Zimbabwe dollar was collapsing.
And then there were the borrowers. If you owed a fixed amount of Zimbabwe dollars, inflation shrank your debt to nothing. A loan that once looked big could be repaid with the price of a newspaper.
Finally, the clearest winners of all. People who held foreign currency, or who had access to the official exchange rate and could swap at a price far better than everyone else.

But owning things wasn't a perfect escape either. You can't eat a house, and you can't pay for a bus ticket with half a cow. Plenty of people who owned land or a home still went hungry, because they had no money that worked for daily life.

The people who did best had both. Real assets to protect their wealth, and a steady source of foreign currency to live on. Usually that meant exporters, people with family abroad, and people close to the system who could get the official exchange rate.
So the pattern is simple and brutal. Hyperinflation moves wealth from people who save in money, to people who own things and owe money.
The careful saver loses. The heavily indebted asset owner wins. Which is the opposite of what we usually teach as good financial behaviour.
In January 2009, Zimbabwe allowed people to use foreign currencies. By April, the Zimbabwe dollar had effectively been abandoned. US dollars and rand took over.
And almost overnight, prices stopped rising. No clever policy. People simply stopped using the thing that was broken.

In 2015, the central bank formally closed the chapter. Old balances were swapped at thirty five quadrillion Zimbabwe dollars for one US dollar. Anyone with up to one hundred and seventy five quadrillion in the bank got a flat five dollars.
But the story doesn't end there. In 2019, Zimbabwe brought back a local currency, and inflation came back with it.
In April 2024, it launched another one, the ZiG, short for Zimbabwe Gold, backed by gold and reserves. By the end of September, it had been cut by more than forty percent.

Zimbabwe isn't unique. Germany went through this in 1923, Hungary in 1946, Yugoslavia in the 1990s, Venezuela more recently. The details change, but the recipe is almost always the same. A government spends far more than it collects, the economy that produces real goods shrinks, and the central bank fills the gap by printing.

And it starts slowly. Zimbabwe's inflation didn't jump to billions overnight. It crept up for years, while each new fix, a price control here, a few zeros removed there, treated the symptom and not the cause.

Because a currency isn't really paper, or gold. It's trust. People have to believe that the money they earn today will still buy something tomorrow. Once that trust is gone, it's very hard to print it back.

Remember the hundred trillion dollar note? It couldn't buy a week of groceries when it was printed. Today, collectors pay tens, sometimes hundreds of US dollars for one. It's worth more as a souvenir of a dead currency than it ever was as money.

So what's the lesson for the rest of us? Most countries today aim for low, steady inflation, around two percent a year. That still means your cash slowly loses value. Zimbabwe is just the same process, sped up until you can watch it happen.
So here's my question for you. If your own currency started losing value every week, what would you hold instead? Cash, gold, property, foreign currency, or something else?
